author: Sharon Zhang
title: Israeli Plan for Crocodile Moat for Prison for Palestinians Blocked for Animal Welfare
content: An Israeli court has temporarily blocked a plan, cooked up by far right minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, to construct a moat full of crocodiles around a notoriously abusive prison that holds Palestinians. The injunction was issued on Sunday against the transfer of crocodiles to the facility in response to a petition filed over concerns that the crocodiles would be harmed or mistreated.

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: State surveillance adds to teachers’ multiple burden
content:
CAGAYAN DE ORO — A public school head expressed her strong denunciation as she narrated the recent series of surveillance by alleged state agents to some teachers in Pitogo, Zamboanga del Sur.

“If they won’t stop red-tagging, profiling, tailing, harassing, and intimidating us, we will file a case,” Liza Idiang, chairperson of the Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT) Zamboanga Peninsula Region, told Bulatlat in an interview.

Idiang, a public school head at Balongbalong Elementary School in Pitogo town, said the surveillance started on July 25, when two individuals who introduced themselves as personnel of the Philippine National Police (PNP) went to her residence, asking for her whereabouts.

Since she was in Pagadian City that time, the alleged police personnel proceeded to the residence of another teacher, asking if they were planning to stage a protest action for the State of the Nation Address (SONA) of Ferdinand Marcos Jr., and if the latter was recruited by Idiang to join ACT.

The residence of another ACT Zamboanga Peninsula member in Pitogo, Idiang said, was also allegedly visited by state agents.

Another person who also introduced himself as police personnel visited Idiang’s house on July 26. This time, she was able to confront the person. The latter allegedly uttered red-tagging remarks against their organization.

“If this is not the right time for you to express your concerns and demands, for us, this is the right time. You are not blind or deaf to not know all of the happenings in our country today,” Idiang told Bulatlat in the vernacular, as she recalled what she said to the alleged police.

Later that day, another alleged state agent went to Idiang’s house, apologizing as he was the one who shared the information about a possible protest that was supposed to be led by Idiang.

However, the surveillance did not stop there. On July 27, the day of the SONA, some teachers in Balongbalong Elementary School displayed their tarpaulins that highlighted their calls for a salary increase and education funding. On that day, the teachers’ rights advocate said two individuals who introduced themselves as members of the Citizen Armed Force Geographical Unit (CAFGU), an auxiliary force of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP), entered the school premises, asking about their activities.

Idiang said suspected state agents allegedly continued their surveillance until July 30.

“They are the ones who further damaged our mental health. We are already exhausted, and our mental health was unstable, yet they just added to the burden,” she said in the vernacular.

Bulatlat sent an email to Police Regional Office 9 to ask for comment, but there is no response as of this writing.

Read: #HandsOffOurTeachers | Alliance mulls filing charges against police

In a statement, ACT Philippines condemned the harassment, highlighting the negative impacts of this continuing surveillance and intimidation on the lives, liberty, and security of teachers who were just exercising their rights.

The group further stressed that such incidents contradict Executive Order 97 (Adopting the Omnibus Guidelines on the Exercise of Freedom of Association and Civil Liberties) issued by Marcos Jr. last year.

“The government should direct its resources toward prosecuting corrupt officials, plunderers, and those responsible for the wholesale misuse of public funds. Those who steal from the Filipino people should be the objects of relentless pursuit, not those courageously asserting legitimate democratic demands,” said Ruby Bernardo, ACT Philippines chairperson.

The teachers’ alliance called on the Department of Education to defend their teachers’ right to organize. It also urged the Civil Service Commission and the Commission on Human Rights to launch an independent investigation and hold those responsible accountable. (RVO)

author: Felicia Anthonio
title: #KeepItOn: Government of Zambia must uphold human rights and ensure unrestricted internet access throughout the upcoming elections
content:
For the attention of President Hakainde Hichilema, President of the Republic of Zambia

CC: Eng. Collins Mbulo, Director General of the Zambia Information and Communications Technology Authority (ZICTA); Eng. Dr. Brilliant Haabenzu, Permanent Secretary Ministry of Technology and Science; Mrs Mwenya Kaela Bwalya (Legal), Permanent Secretary Secretary Ministry of Justice; Dr. Pamela Towela Sambo, Chairperson, Zambia Human Rights Commission; Webster Malido, Director General, Independent Broadcasting Authority (IBA);  Mulilo Dimas Kabesha, SC, Attorney General of Zambia; Friday Musiyalike Nyambe, Zambia Security Intelligence Services; Graphel Musamba, Inspector General of Police; Schmidt Chintu, Director General Zambia Cyber Security Agency; Abbad Reda, Chief Executive Officer, MTN Zambia; Hussam Baday, Managing Director of Airtel Zambia; Jason Mwanza, Chief Executive Officer, Zamtel; Leah Nakazwe Kooma, Chief Executive Officer, Liquid Intelligent Technologies; Marius Van Vuuren, Country Manager, Paratus.

Around the world, governments deploy internet shutdowns to interfere with election outcomes and undermine democratic participation. This practice harms human rights — we cannot allow it to become normalized. Ahead of the upcoming general  elections, we urge the Republic of Zambia to #KeepItOn.

We, the undersigned organizations and members of the #KeepItOn coalition — a global network of over 370 organizations from 106 countries working to end internet shutdowns — appeal to you, President Hakainde Hichilema, to ensure that people in Zambia have unfettered access to the internet, digital platforms, and all other communication channels throughout the upcoming elections on August 13, 2026.

The #KeepItOn coalition welcomes the Ministry of Technology and Science’s commitment to not shut down the internet during the general election and urges your office to issue a directive to the relevant institutions, including the ZICTA, the Ministry of Technology and Science, and all internet service providers (ISPs) operating in the country, to refrain from disrupting access to the internet and digital platforms and to ensure unrestricted access during the electoral cycle and beyond. We further note the government’s statement that it was unable to establish the cause of the 2021 internet shutdown, and urge authorities to continue a transparent investigation into that disruption.

As the people of Zambia prepare to vote, we underscore the critical importance of access to information, freedom of expression and freedom of assembly. These rights are essential to inclusive participation and a cornerstone of free, fair, and credible elections. During elections, the free flow of information is also a lifeline that must be protected to allow scrutiny of the entire process. The internet and digital communication platforms have given people unprecedented access to election information and enabled them to express their opinions, interact with candidates, and actively participate in electoral campaigns. Journalists, human rights defenders, and election observers also rely on the internet and digital platforms to carry out their critical role of monitoring, documenting, and reporting on election processes.

Zambia’s shrinking civic space

Access Now and the #KeepItOn coalition have also noted with concern the enactment of the Cybercrimes Act and Cybersecurity Act , both of which have the potential to further restrict freedom of expression in the country. These laws come at a time when freedom of expression in Zambia is under attack , with journalists and members of the opposition facing arrest for publications and public utterances perceived to be critical of the government.

We commend the decision of the President not to assent to the Public Gathering Bill, 2026 , after its enactment by Parliament The bill, as it is, stands to further restrict the freedom of association and assembly through vague and overbroad provisions. We reiterate the appeal of the UN Special Rapporteur on the Rights to Freedom of Assembly and Association for your government to ensure full protection of the rights to freedom of peaceful assembly and association throughout the electoral cycle.

Zambia’s history of internet shutdowns

Zambian authorities reportedly blocked access to social media platforms and messaging apps including WhatsApp, Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram during the August 12,  2021 elections . The shutdown was eventually lifted after civil society organizations challenged the constitutionality of the shutdown order in court. Following this legal challenge, the ZICTA entered into a consent judgment in which it committed to not acting outside its authority to interrupt internet access in the country, and to informing the public of the reason for any future interruption within 36 hours. Similar election-related disruptions were documented in 2016.

In 2020, Freedom House reported another two-day shutdown . Government officials attributed the disruption to heavy rains; however, officials of the United Party for National Development (UPND) alleged the government was responsible for the restriction. There have also been instances of targeted blockings of websites belonging to media outlets operating in the country.

Internet shutdowns harm human rights, worsen crises, and disrupt democratic processes

Internet shutdowns violate fundamental human rights, including freedom of opinion and expression, access to information, freedom of assembly, and the right to vote and to participate in democratic processes such as elections. Cutting off internet access during elections limits the flow of crucial, timely information, silences dissent and opposition voices, and hinders scrutiny and transparency of the electoral process. Shutdowns also create information vacuums, further fueling the spread of hateful and inciting speech, misinformation, and disinformation.

Moreover, shutdowns during elections make it extremely difficult for journalists to report on the ground and verify information with their sources, leaving people inside and outside Zambia without access to trustworthy, credible information. Shutdowns also make it onerous for journalists and human rights defenders to document and verify atrocities committed, thereby enabling perpetrators to evade accountability .

Shutdowns have been proven to hinder vital election-monitoring work undertaken by election observers, including local and international election observer groups, political parties, media outlets, and civil society. Reports from regional and sub-regional election observers underscore the severe impact of these shutdowns on election monitoring, raising questions about the integrity of the election outcomes. For instance, the African Union Election Observation Mission’s preliminary report highlights that Tanzania’s five-day internet blackout during the October 2025 elections blocked citizens’ access to information and severely limited election observers’ ability to monitor critical aspects of the process, including voting, polling station closures, and vote counting.

Additionally, internet shutdowns disrupt people’s lives and daily activities. The 2021 shutdown in Zambia, for instance, brought many economic activities and businesses to a halt: people could not access information, journalists were unable to carry out their work,  and businesses lost opportunities.

Internet shutdowns contravene national and international laws

Internet shutdowns contravene national and international human rights law. The Constitution of Zambia, as well as regional and international frameworks such as the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) and the African Charter on Human and Peoples’ Rights , to which Zambia is signatory, protects and promotes the rights of freedom of opinion and expression, assembly, and access to information — both online and offline. The Declaration of Principles on Freedom of Expression and Access to Information in Africa 2019 also calls on States not to “engage in or condone any disruption of access to the internet and other digital technologies for segments of the public or an entire population.”

The African Commission on Human and Peoples’ Rights (ACHPR) has repeatedly underscored the importance of internet connectivity. In 2024, through Resolution 580 , the ACHPR called on state parties to ensure open and secure internet access before, during, and after elections. The Commission recently raised concerns about the nationwide internet shutdowns in Tanzania and threats to shut down the internet in Uganda during the countries’ respective elections. It reiterated the importance of the internet in advancing human and peoples’ rights in Africa, particularly given that, for elections to be free, fair and credible, the electorate must have access to information at all stages of the electoral process.

Moreover, in 2023, the Freedom Online Coalition (FOC) condemned election-related shutdowns and underscored that “protecting, respecting, and promoting human rights is essential to foster free and fair elections.” It added that by “obstructing the free flow of information, opinions, and expression […] internet shutdowns threaten the legitimacy of the electoral process” and ultimately undermine public trust. The UN Secretary General and other experts have also affirmed that “blanket internet shutdowns and generic blocking and filtering of services are considered by United Nations human rights mechanisms to violate international human rights law.”  The ECOWAS Community Court of Justice has issued four separate judgments finding that the use of internet shutdowns violates human rights, including freedom of expression, in Togo , Nigeria , Senegal , and Guinea . In countries such as Sudan and Zimbabwe, the High Court has ruled that internet shutdowns are unconstitutional.

Telcos must respect human rights

Under the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises , telecommunications companies are responsible for preventing or mitigating potential human rights harms they may cause or contribute to, and for providing remedies when and if such harms occur. Telecommunications companies and ISPs operating in Zambia — including MTN Zambia, Airtel Zambia, Liquid Intelligent Technologies, and all other ISPs — must resist any shutdown orders from the government and provide quality, open, and secure access to the internet and digital communication tools throughout the elections and beyond.

Internet shutdowns should never become the norm, whether in Zambia or elsewhere. We encourage businesses in Zambia to integrate the UN Guiding Principles and the OECD Guidelines when responding to censorship and network-disruption requests in any market where they operate.

We call on you, President Hichilema, to:

Publicly assure people in Zambia that access to the internet, including social media and other digital communications platforms, will remain unrestricted during and after the election.

Call upon the respective institutions and authorities to refrain from ordering any disruption of telecommunications services, social media platforms, or other digital communication platforms throughout the elections.

Ensure that telecommunications and ISPs implement all necessary measures to provide high-quality, secure, unrestricted, and uninterrupted internet access throughout the election period and beyond, in line with their quality-of-service and license conditions.

Honor the 2021 consent judgment entered by ZICTA; and ensure that the authority, telecommunications, and ISPs inform people in Zambia of any potential technical disruptions during the elections, and take all reasonable steps to remedy any such disruptions likely to impact their service quality.

Uphold human rights and ensure that the Cybercrimes Act and the Cybersecurity Act do not become deliberate tools to suppress freedom of expression before, during and after the elections.

The #KeepItOn coalition urges your office to affirm the commitment made by the Ministry of Technology and Science by assuring the people of Zambia of open, secure and inclusive internet and respect for fundamental rights throughout the election. Please let us know how we can support your efforts to uphold an accessible internet for all in Zambia.

title: Soft Digital Repression: New Challenges and Strategies for Resistance
content:
For this reason, the battle over technology remains part of the broader struggle against domination and exploitation, and for democracy, equality, freedom, and a socialist alternative. Returning the human being to the center of digital decision-making remains a fundamental condition for building a future in which technology serves society rather than the accumulation of capital.

During the recent assault on Gaza, thousands of activists witnessed their posts deleted or their accounts restricted simply for documenting Israeli occupation crimes or expressing solidarity with the Palestinian people. This is far from an isolated phenomenon. In India, the government issued emergency orders to block dozens of accounts during the farmers' protests, while human rights organizations documented the suspension of accounts belonging to large numbers of journalists and activists merely for criticizing government policies. Many felt helpless and furious, as their voices seemed to be deliberately pushed to the margins. These cases offer a clear illustration of what can today be called "soft digital repression."

This form of repression does not always manifest as direct blocking or public arrest. It operates through invisible algorithms and digital systems, reshaping the digital space in ways that determine what reaches audiences and what gets marginalized. With the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence, these mechanisms have grown increasingly complex and far-reaching. This raises a pressing question: how does this system work, and how can it be confronted?

Large digital corporations collect vast amounts of data systematically, using artificial intelligence to analyze it and classify users according to behavioral patterns, intellectual orientations, and political inclinations. Through carefully designed algorithms, left-wing, progressive, and human rights content can be restricted without any need for direct deletion. From the user's perspective, low engagement appears to stem from audience indifference, when in reality it may be the result of algorithmic mechanisms controlling the level of reach and visibility.

Many have experienced this firsthand: a significant post is written and reaches only a limited number of followers. Numerous studies have examined the phenomenon of the filter bubble, whereby users are gradually isolated within information environments that reinforce their pre-existing views while limiting their exposure to critical or alternative content. The 2021 Facebook leaks revealed internal discussions concerning content management and the influence of algorithms on the public sphere. The Brookings Institution has documented how digital platforms contribute to deepening political polarization and entrenching ideological dominance.

Over time, many users begin practicing what might be called "voluntary self-surveillance," imposing restrictions on themselves out of fear of bans or declining reach. This fear reshapes the nature of public discourse and gradually transforms the digital space into a more controlled environment, one that serves the interests of the forces dominating the digital infrastructure.

Through the constant flow of content, algorithms contribute to generating a sense of helplessness and loss of hope in the possibility of change, by repeatedly emphasizing the failures of progressive experiments and presenting the existing capitalist order as the only viable option. At the same time, individualism and personal success solutions are promoted as the primary path for addressing social problems, while consumer culture and individual achievement are presented as the practical alternative to collective action and political organization. The result is the isolation of individuals, the weakening of collective bonds, and the transformation of shared social concerns into personal responsibilities.

When covert surveillance or frustration proves insufficient, the system reaches more explicit levels of digital exclusion. Activists and journalists suddenly find their accounts suspended or blocked without prior warning, with these measures justified by generic phrases such as "violating community standards," even though the targeted content is in many cases documentation of human rights violations or war crimes.

In other cases, the situation reaches what can only be described as "digital assassination": the complete erasure of the digital presence of individuals or entire institutions. The targeting of Palestinian content stands as one of the most contested examples, with human rights organizations and researchers having documented numerous instances of post deletions and account restrictions linked to coverage of violations, alongside a striking inconsistency in the application of content rules across different parties.

If soft digital repression seeks to limit the potential for resistance, organization, and free expression, then confronting it begins with reconsidering technology itself as an arena of social and political struggle.

This requires pushing for greater transparency and democratic oversight of large digital corporations, and enacting legislation that protects privacy, criminalizes political surveillance, and mandates disclosure of algorithmic decision-making mechanisms.

The response cannot be limited to legislation alone. There is also a need to build digital left-wing internationals and cross-border solidarity networks that expose digital violations and defend rights and freedoms in the online space. Users and civil society institutions can also exert pressure on companies involved in developing or selling surveillance technologies used against activists, journalists, and dissidents.

It is equally important to support free and open-source software, and to develop alternative platforms that are more transparent and subject to community oversight, so that technology is used to protect rights, expose violations, and strengthen democratic participation.

Left-wing and progressive organizations should also develop their own digital tools, ranging from encryption and privacy protection technologies to awareness campaigns that expose the inner workings of algorithms and their political and social impact.

If the recurring experiences of Palestinian content restrictions, alongside other cases that have targeted left-wing, progressive, and human rights voices across different parts of the world, reveal an important dimension of the problem, they also confirm that alternatives are possible.

The issue is not about rejecting artificial intelligence or digital technology. The question concerns who owns this technology, how it is governed, and in whose interest it operates. Transforming artificial intelligence into a tool that serves society and whose use is subject to democratic oversight can open new horizons for participation, organization, and solidarity.

The internet is not merely a global marketplace for advertising and data. It is a social, political, and cultural space that can contribute to building new forms of collective action and struggle for social justice.

For this reason, the battle over technology remains part of the broader struggle against domination and exploitation, and for democracy, equality, freedom, and a socialist alternative. Returning the human being to the center of digital decision-making remains a fundamental condition for building a future in which technology serves society rather than the accumulation of capital.

******************************************

Rezgar Akrawi is a leftist writer and researcher focused on technology, AI, the digital revolution, and the development of contemporary leftist thought and practice in response to these transformations. He works as an expert in systems development and e-governance and is a theorist of the concept of the “Digital - Electronic Left.”

title: No new mandate for Frontex!
content:
The European Commission is set to publish a proposal for a new Frontex regulation in the second half of this year. The review is expected to expand the mandate of the EU border agency, strengthening its role in deportations, border externalisation, and the collection and processing of personal data. It is also likely to broaden the agency’s remit beyond border ‘security’ and control to include responding to so-called “hybrid threats”, while further expanding its Standing Corps and doubling its budget. These developments are particularly concerning given Frontex’s increasingly central role in the EU’s violent, human rights-violating border regime.




Mandate review




Frontex began operating in 2005 as a small agency tasked with coordinating border ‘security’ and control at the EU’s external borders. Since 2015 in particular, its role, mandate, organisation and budget have expanded rapidly. The agency has started building up its own armed border guard corps, acquired its own surveillance equipment, taken on a more active role in deportations, and launched operations in non-EU countries. The last revision of the Frontex mandate, in 

2019

, significantly increased the agency’s powers.




In July 2024, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen presented her 

Political Guidelines 2024–2029

, outlining the programme for the new Commission. She announced plans to “strengthen Frontex, notably to equip it with state-of-the-art technology for surveillance and situational awareness, along with its own equipment and personnel to ensure it can protect our borders in all circumstances”. She also proposed tripling the size of the Standing Corps to 30,000 border guards. These plans were reiterated in the EU’s 

Internal Security Strategy

 (April 2025) and 

Asylum and Migration Management Strategy

 (January 2026), both of which also emphasise expanding Frontex’s operational role in deportations.




In summer 2025 the Commission launched a 

public consultation

 on updating the Frontex Regulation, with the aim of presenting a legislative proposal in the third quarter of 2026. Meanwhile, the Commission’s proposal for the next EU-budget, the Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) for 2028–2034, 

includes

 €11.9 billion to Frontex – doubling the agency’s budget under the current 2021–2027 MFF.




Proposed changes




Although the content of the Commission’s proposal is not yet known, it has indicated that it intends to 

address

 several key areas, including:







Expansion of its workforce and equipment pool







Frontex is currently building its own 10,000-strong armed 

Standing Border Guard Corps

, which is deployed in Frontex operations both inside and outside the EU and assists member states with border control, border surveillance and deportations. As noted above, the Commission has proposed increasing the corps to 30,000 personnel. 




Initially dependent on equipment provided by member states, Frontex has been able to purchase or lease its own equipment since 2011. Following budget increases from 2017 onwards, it has signed several major contracts, particularly for aerial surveillance, although debates over its procurement strategy have delayed many plans. The Commission now intends to further expand Frontex’s own equipment pool, especially its surveillance capabilities.




Frontex’s expansion of surveillance across EU external borders and beyond has largely 

served

 the detection, apprehension and often subsequent pushback of people on the move. Rarely has such equipment served search and rescue.







A larger role in deportations, inside and outside the EU







Frontex’s involvement in deportations has evolved from coordinating joint return flights at the request of groups of member states to taking a far more active operational 

role

, including initiating deportations itself. In 2025, it assisted in the deportation of more than 60,000 people. Under the EU’s new 

Deportation Regulation

, adopted in June 2026, Frontex’s responsibilities will be 

expanded

 further, covering support for deportations, information exchange, cooperation with non-EU countries, and implementation of a new digital return architecture.




In connection with the controversial plans to establish ‘

return hubs

‘ – detention centers in non-EU countries where people on the move can be transferred to from the EU – the Commission 

may

 also include provisions allowing Frontex to assist with deportations from one non-EU country to another as part of the new regulation.







Expanded powers to collect, process and share personal data







The EU operates a range of biometric identity databases in the field of border and migration management. Although most are managed by the agency 

eu-LISA

, Frontex has gained increasing access to them, also in the context of a longer running 

project

 to make them 

interoperable

.




According

 to the Commission, “the rules on processing relevant data, including personal data, are complex, but also incomplete, and hinder Frontex’s work on situational awareness, cross-border crime prevention and return activities”. This suggests that the proposed regulation will seek to simplify and expand Frontex’s ability to collect, process and share personal data. Such changes would also be in line with the new 

working arrangement

 between Europol and Frontex signed in July 2026, and the new Europol proposal of June 2026 that would allow Frontex to have access on a hit/no-hit basis and on condition of reciprocity to Europol systems (Article 80, Europol Regulation Proposal 2026/0165 (COD)). 




The increasing morphing of databases set up for differing purposes, such as migration control and criminal investigations, gives rise to concerns regarding privacy, data protection, bias (including racial profiling) and respect for fundamental rights. Broader access to the Schengen Information System, which under the new Deportation Regulation will be used as the register for issued deportation orders and for people on the move marked as security threats, for example makes every law enforcement officer a potential ‘migrant hunter’.







Expanded cooperation with and operations in non-EU countries







Over the past decade, the EU has increasingly focused on border externalisation, relying on non-EU countries to prevent people on the move from ever reaching the EU’s external borders. Frontex has played an expanding 

role

 in this process, moving beyond working arrangements – primarily focused on the readmission of deported people – via the exchange of intelligence, risk analysis and (biometric) data to conducting its own border operations in several non-EU countries. 




As part of the regulation review, the Commission 

argues

 that “the rules governing Frontex’s cooperation with third countries are not suited to the diversity of third countries that it has to work together with. Moreover, they are not sufficiently flexible, which limits Frontex’s ability to adjust its operational support to emerging needs”, and calls for the “prioritisation and expansion of operations in third countries”.




An ad hoc coalition of ten member states, including Poland and Spain, 

echoed

 this position in a non-paper published in February 2026, arguing that “a stronger Frontex presence is needed in third countries, particularly in countries of origin and transit”. It is therefore likely that the Commission’s proposal will include a framework allowing broader and more flexible cooperation agreements with non-EU countries. Apart from the direct consequences for people on the move this also often leads to legitimizing and strengthening authoritarian regimes, reinforcing their capacities for internal repression as well.







Situational awareness and ‘hybrid threats’







The Commission also 

suggests

 to introduce legislative measures on “situational awareness to enable, among other things, a faster and better response to hybrid threats”. This could broaden Frontex’s remit beyond migration management and cross-border crime.




Discussion regarding ‘hybrid threats’ so far has primarily focused on the highly problematic narrative of so-called ‘instrumentalisation of migration’, of which for example Belarus has been accused. Describing people on the move as ‘instruments’ (or even ‘weapons’) of adversary governments conflates migration with a defence agency and further legitimizes violent responses against them. 




On top of that there have also been proposals to involve Frontex in for example responding to drone incursions or attacks on infrastructure. Member states 

reportedl

y hold widely differing views on these proposals, so it remains unclear how far they will be reflected in the revised mandate. Any move in this direction, however, would push Frontex further into the 

military sphere

 and deepen its contribution to the EU’s mass 

militarisation

 agenda.




No need for (more) Frontex




All of the major elements expected to feature in the revised Frontex Regulation point towards further expansion of the agency’s mandate, operational role, geographical presence – both inside and outside the EU – and institutional infrastructure. This would only worsen the many issues associated with the agency, including its responsibility for violence, pushbacks and human rights violations, its cooperation with authoritarian regimes and its poor handling of personal data, as well as the lack of accountability and the impunity enjoyed by its personnel for all this. Even without a new mandate, Frontex’s activities, capabilities and presence have 

expanded

 rapidly in recent years, aggravating many of these structural flaws and the overall fortification of the border, 

resulting

 in deaths and disappearances.




During the review process, some NGOs and Members of the European Parliament will undoubtedly once again call for stronger transparency, accountability and oversight. Previous efforts have proven woefully insufficient, symbolized by the Fundamental Rights Officer, which has no institutional independence nor any enforcement power. However, such proposals fail to address the underlying structure. Frontex is fulfilling the role assigned to it by the EU and its member states: serving as the operational flagship of the EU’s violent, human rights-abusing border regime. The core problem is the agency’s existence itself. Frontex does not need a new mandate or a new regulation. It does not need reform. It needs to be abolished.
